Lecture 02 · Module 2 · Robot Manipulator Dynamics

Energy-Based Approach to Robot Dynamics

Lagrangian mechanics and systematic dynamic modeling for multi-link manipulators.

Module 2 of N Prerequisites Forward kinematics · Jacobians · Matrix calculus Leads to Module 3 — Full Lagrangian derivation
In this module we trade free-body diagrams for scalars. Instead of chasing every constraint force through a kinematic chain, we'll write down kinetic and potential energy, form the Lagrangian, and let Euler-Lagrange do the bookkeeping. By the end you'll see why $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ falls out almost automatically — and why every modern industrial controller is built on top of this idea.

§ 0.0

What this lecture covers

Orientation

This module builds the energy-based framework for robot dynamics. We start by asking why energy methods beat force methods for multi-link systems, then assemble the pieces: kinetic and potential energy for a kinematic chain, generalized coordinates, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, and the Euler-Lagrange equations.

From there we'll see how velocity kinematics feed the kinetic energy expression, how the inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ emerges as a quadratic form, and how the standard robot equation $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ falls out of the derivation — with each term having a clear physical meaning.

We close with a self-assessment on a 2-DOF planar arm and a look at how this theory powers real industrial controllers.

Think of this as the moment robot dynamics stops being a wall of free-body diagrams and starts being something you can derive systematically — even for arms you've never seen before.

Learning objectives

Master energy fundamentals, the Lagrangian framework, generalized coordinates, Euler-Lagrange equations, and the systematic derivation of robot dynamic equations.

§ 1.0

Why energy methods beat force methods

Motivation

Force-based and energy-based dynamics are mathematically equivalent — they produce the same final equations. The difference is the path to those equations.

For a single pendulum or a particle, Newton-Euler is intuitive: draw the free-body diagram, sum forces, done. But once you have a multi-link robot with several degrees of freedom, force methods force you to track constraint forces at every joint, manage vector forces and torques in many frames, and untangle interaction forces between links. Sign errors and missing coupling terms become routine.

Energy methods work with scalars. You compute kinetic and potential energy, form the Lagrangian, and apply a fixed procedure. Constraint forces simply vanish from the final equations — they do no work on admissible motions, so the formalism eliminates them automatically.

The real advantage isn't elegance — it's that the same five steps work for a 2-DOF planar arm and a 7-DOF surgical robot. That's why every dynamics textbook and every robotics toolbox builds on Lagrange.

Newton-Euler (force-based)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector bookkeeping across frames, and large coupled systems prone to sign errors.

Lagrange (energy-based)

Scalar energies, automatic constraint elimination, generalized coordinates, and a well-defined procedure that is easy to automate.

3-DOF arm comparison

Force method: 6 equations per link plus constraint elimination. Energy method: 3 scalar $T_i$, 3 scalar $V_i$, one $L = T - V$, then Euler-Lagrange. Same answer — far less pain.

Interactive · pick a method Try this on for size: choose Newton-Euler or Lagrange for a 1-, 2-, or 3-link arm and watch the equation count, constraint forces, and frame transformations light up side by side. The two paths converge on the same equations — but one of them is dramatically shorter.
§ 2.0

Kinetic energy in multi-link systems

Energy · T

Kinetic energy in robotics is not the $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ of elementary physics. Every link has both translational kinetic energy (from its center-of-mass velocity) and rotational kinetic energy (from spinning about its center of mass), and the two are coupled through the kinematic chain.

When joint 1 moves, every subsequent link moves with it, each picking up velocity contributions from every joint between itself and the base. This is the velocity coupling that gives robot dynamics their characteristic nonlinearity and cross-terms.

Kinetic energy formula

For a robot with $n$ links: $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right]$. Here $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the CoM velocity, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ the angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ the inertia tensor about the CoM.

Where the coupling lives

Both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on the velocities of all joints from the base to link $i$. That dependency is the source of every coupling term in the inertia matrix.

Interactive · animated coupling Drive $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ on a planar arm and watch each link's translational and rotational kinetic energy stream into the total. You'll see exactly how downstream links inherit velocity from every upstream joint.
§ 3.0

Potential energy and configuration dependence

Energy · V

Potential energy in robotics is primarily gravitational and depends on position only, not velocity — which makes it considerably simpler than kinetic energy.

The key insight is that potential energy is strongly configuration-dependent. An extended horizontal arm stores far more gravitational potential energy than the same arm folded vertically, and the gradient of $V$ with respect to joint angles is exactly the gravitational torque that actuators must overcome.

Gravity compensation in any modern controller is just $\partial V / \partial q_i$ — the same quantity you'd compute by hand here. The math is the implementation.

Potential energy formula

$V = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \mathbf{g}^T \mathbf{r}_i$ where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration vector (typically $[0, 0, -9.81]^T$ m/s$^2$) and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the CoM position of link $i$.

Reference frame choice

You're free to pick any reference height; the equations of motion depend only on differences. A smart choice can collapse several terms to zero.

Interactive · build $V$ Construct $V$ for a 2-DOF planar arm by dragging each link's centre of mass to a height and watching the $m_i g h_i$ terms snap into a live sum. Then sweep $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and watch $V$ change — along with the gravity torque $\partial V/\partial q_i$ at each joint.
§ 4.0

The Lagrangian and generalized coordinates

Framework

Generalized coordinates are any independent parameters that completely specify the configuration. For robots, the natural choice is the joint variables: angles $\theta_i$ for revolute joints, displacements $d_i$ for prismatic joints. A robot with $n$ joints has $n$ degrees of freedom and $n$ generalized coordinates — a minimal, complete description.

The Lagrangian is the scalar function

$$L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q})$$

It's the difference between kinetic and potential energy. Systems evolve along the path that extremizes the time integral of $L$ (the action) — and that variational principle is exactly what produces the Euler-Lagrange equations.

Why joint variables are special

Joint coordinates are minimal (no redundant parameters), automatically satisfy kinematic constraints, and correspond directly to actuator readings — so theory and hardware speak the same language.

Interpretation

$L$ measures the excess of kinetic energy over potential energy. Nature picks trajectories that extremize the time integral of this excess.

§ 5.0

The Euler-Lagrange equations

Procedure

The Euler-Lagrange equations turn the Lagrangian into equations of motion. For each generalized coordinate $q_i$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = \tau_i$$

where $\tau_i$ is the generalized force (joint torque for revolute joints, force for prismatic). The procedure is mechanical: write $T$ and $V$, form $L = T - V$, take the required partials, and simplify.

Once you've written $L$, the rest is calculus. That's the whole appeal — derivation becomes bookkeeping, not insight.

The five-step recipe

1) Express $T$ and $V$ in generalized coordinates. 2) Form $L = T - V$. 3) Compute $\partial L / \partial \dot{q}_i$ and $\partial L / \partial q_i$. 4) Differentiate the velocity partial with respect to time. 5) Substitute into Euler-Lagrange and simplify.

Worked sketch: 2-DOF planar arm

Choose $q_1 = \theta_1$, $q_2 = \theta_2$. Link 1 rotates with $\dot{\theta}_1$; link 2 picks up coupled motion from both joints. The resulting equations are nonlinear, coupled, and capture inertial coupling, Coriolis/centrifugal effects, and gravity loading — even for this minimal system.

Interactive · derive it yourself Now you walk through the recipe. Pick a production rule at each step — write $T$, write $V$, form $L$, take partials, apply Euler-Lagrange — and the expression tree grows until you've produced the equation of motion for a 1-DOF pendulum, then a 2-DOF arm.
§ 6.0

Velocity kinematics for energy calculations

Jacobians

To compute $T$ you need link velocities, and those follow from the kinematic chain. The linear velocity of link $i$'s center of mass is

$$\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j} \dot{q}_j = \mathbf{J}_{vi}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ is the velocity Jacobian for the CoM of link $i$.

Angular velocities follow joint-type rules: a revolute joint $j$ with rate $\dot{q}_j$ contributes $\dot{q}_j$ (about its axis) to every link downstream; a prismatic joint contributes zero. So the total angular velocity of link $i$ is the vector sum of contributions from all revolute joints between it and the base.

3-DOF planar example

All revolute, planar: $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 = \dot{q}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_3 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2 + \dot{q}_3$. Each subsequent link inherits velocity from more joints — that's where coupling terms come from.

Practical takeaway

Get the Jacobians right and the kinetic energy expression writes itself. Most errors in Lagrangian derivations trace back to a sloppy velocity expression.

§ 7.0

The inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Structure

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into the kinetic energy formula yields a quadratic form in joint velocities:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is the inertia matrix (sometimes called the mass matrix), with elements

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right]$$

Reading $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Diagonal $D_{ii}$: effective inertia felt by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves. Off-diagonal $D_{ij}$: inertial coupling between joints $i$ and $j$. The whole matrix changes with configuration.

Mathematical properties

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — kinetic energy is non-negative, and zero only when $\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0}$. This guarantees physically consistent, well-posed dynamics.

Interactive · pick a configuration Slide $\theta_2$ on a 2-DOF arm and watch all four entries of the inertia matrix update in real time, with the eigenvalues plotted alongside. You'll see why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent — and where the coupling lives.
§ 8.0

Deriving the standard robot equation

Result

Plugging $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ into Euler-Lagrange and taking the required derivatives produces the standard form of the robot dynamic equation:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$$

Each term has a distinct physical origin:

  • $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ — inertial term, straight from $T$.
  • $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis and centrifugal terms, arising from the time-derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ minus the position-partial of $T$.
  • $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \partial V / \partial \mathbf{q}$ — gravitational term, from $V$.

Inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Comes directly from kinetic energy.

Coriolis/centrifugal $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$

Quadratic in velocities: $h_i = \sum_j \sum_k h_{ijk} \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k$ with Christoffel-style symbols $h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right)$.

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$

$c_i = \partial V / \partial q_i$. Conservative, velocity-independent, the literal gradient of potential energy.

Why this form matters

Every modern model-based controller — computed-torque, inverse dynamics, passivity-based — references this exact decomposition. Get $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ right and you can implement any of them.

Self-check · four short questions Before moving on, confirm you can name where each term comes from, what it depends on, and why constraint forces never appear. Get all four and you're ready for Module 3.
§ 9.0

Self-assessment: 2-DOF planar arm

Practice

System. A 2-link planar arm with both link masses concentrated at the distal end (the tip) of each link.

Parameters.

  • Link 1: length $L_1$, mass $m_1$ at its tip.
  • Link 2: length $L_2$, mass $m_2$ at its tip.
  • Joint angles $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ (with $\theta_2$ measured relative to link 1).
  • Neglect link mass distribution and link inertia — assume all mass at the tips.

Tasks.

  1. Kinematics. Write the position of each mass $(m_1, m_2)$ in terms of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$.
  2. Velocities. Compute the velocity of each mass using the chain rule and joint velocities $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.
  3. Kinetic energy. Write the total $T$ of the system (no need to expand).
  4. Potential energy. Write the total gravitational $V$, with gravity acting in the $-y$ direction.
  5. Lagrangian. Form $L = T - V$.

Draw your own schematic and label every point, velocity, and angle. The exercise looks small, but it's the same procedure you'd run on a 7-DOF industrial arm — just with more terms.

Why this exercise matters

This is the smallest non-trivial system that exhibits inertial coupling, Coriolis effects, and configuration-dependent gravity all at once. Master it and the rest scales.

§ 10.0

From theory to industrial controllers

In practice

The energy-based framework isn't an academic exercise — it's the foundation of every modern industrial robot controller. Embedded processors compute $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster as part of real-time control loops.

Downstream applications include trajectory optimization (minimum-time, minimum-energy paths), collision detection via energy monitoring, force limiting for safe human-robot interaction, and predictive maintenance from drive-torque signatures.

Performance gains in practice

Lagrangian-based control delivers position accuracy under 0.1 mm at high speed, 20–40% energy savings over basic PID, 2–3× faster cycle times, and reduced mechanical wear.

Automotive welding case study

Before (PID): ±2 mm, 45 s cycle. After (model-based): ±0.2 mm, 28 s cycle. Result: 35% faster production, 90% accuracy improvement, 25% energy savings.

Looking forward to Module 3

Next module: complete velocity formulation, systematic derivation of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, computation of $\mathbf{h}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, and full worked examples on real robot geometries.

§ 0.0

What this lecture covers

Orientation

This module builds the energy-based framework for robot dynamics. We start by asking why energy methods beat force methods for multi-link systems, then assemble the pieces: kinetic and potential energy for a kinematic chain, generalized coordinates, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, and the Euler-Lagrange equations.

From there we'll see how velocity kinematics feed the kinetic energy expression, how the inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ emerges as a quadratic form, and how the standard robot equation $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ falls out of the derivation — with each term having a clear physical meaning.

We close with a self-assessment on a 2-DOF planar arm and a look at how this theory powers real industrial controllers.

Think of this as the moment robot dynamics stops being a wall of free-body diagrams and starts being something you can derive systematically — even for arms you've never seen before.

Learning objectives

Master energy fundamentals, the Lagrangian framework, generalized coordinates, Euler-Lagrange equations, and the systematic derivation of robot dynamic equations.

§ 1.0

Why energy methods beat force methods

Motivation

Force-based and energy-based dynamics are mathematically equivalent — they produce the same final equations. The difference is the path to those equations.

For a single pendulum or a particle, Newton-Euler is intuitive: draw the free-body diagram, sum forces, done. But once you have a multi-link robot with several degrees of freedom, force methods force you to track constraint forces at every joint, manage vector forces and torques in many frames, and untangle interaction forces between links. Sign errors and missing coupling terms become routine.

Energy methods work with scalars. You compute kinetic and potential energy, form the Lagrangian, and apply a fixed procedure. Constraint forces simply vanish from the final equations — they do no work on admissible motions, so the formalism eliminates them automatically.

The real advantage isn't elegance — it's that the same five steps work for a 2-DOF planar arm and a 7-DOF surgical robot. That's why every dynamics textbook and every robotics toolbox builds on Lagrange.

Newton-Euler (force-based)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector bookkeeping across frames, and large coupled systems prone to sign errors.

Lagrange (energy-based)

Scalar energies, automatic constraint elimination, generalized coordinates, and a well-defined procedure that is easy to automate.

3-DOF arm comparison

Force method: 6 equations per link plus constraint elimination. Energy method: 3 scalar $T_i$, 3 scalar $V_i$, one $L = T - V$, then Euler-Lagrange. Same answer — far less pain.

Interactive · pick a method Try this on for size: choose Newton-Euler or Lagrange for a 1-, 2-, or 3-link arm and watch the equation count, constraint forces, and frame transformations light up side by side. The two paths converge on the same equations — but one of them is dramatically shorter.
§ 2.0

Kinetic energy in multi-link systems

Energy · T

Kinetic energy in robotics is not the $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ of elementary physics. Every link has both translational kinetic energy (from its center-of-mass velocity) and rotational kinetic energy (from spinning about its center of mass), and the two are coupled through the kinematic chain.

When joint 1 moves, every subsequent link moves with it, each picking up velocity contributions from every joint between itself and the base. This is the velocity coupling that gives robot dynamics their characteristic nonlinearity and cross-terms.

Kinetic energy formula

For a robot with $n$ links: $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right]$. Here $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the CoM velocity, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ the angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ the inertia tensor about the CoM.

Where the coupling lives

Both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on the velocities of all joints from the base to link $i$. That dependency is the source of every coupling term in the inertia matrix.

Interactive · animated coupling Drive $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ on a planar arm and watch each link's translational and rotational kinetic energy stream into the total. You'll see exactly how downstream links inherit velocity from every upstream joint.

§ 0.0

What this lecture covers

Orientation

This module builds the energy-based framework for robot dynamics. We start by asking why energy methods beat force methods for multi-link systems, then assemble the pieces: kinetic and potential energy for a kinematic chain, generalized coordinates, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, and the Euler-Lagrange equations.

From there we'll see how velocity kinematics feed the kinetic energy expression, how the inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ emerges as a quadratic form, and how the standard robot equation $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ falls out of the derivation — with each term having a clear physical meaning.

We close with a self-assessment on a 2-DOF planar arm and a look at how this theory powers real industrial controllers.

Think of this as the moment robot dynamics stops being a wall of free-body diagrams and starts being something you can derive systematically — even for arms you've never seen before.

Learning objectives

Master energy fundamentals, the Lagrangian framework, generalized coordinates, Euler-Lagrange equations, and the systematic derivation of robot dynamic equations.

§ 1.0

Why energy methods beat force methods

Motivation

Force-based and energy-based dynamics are mathematically equivalent — they produce the same final equations. The difference is the path to those equations.

For a single pendulum or a particle, Newton-Euler is intuitive: draw the free-body diagram, sum forces, done. But once you have a multi-link robot with several degrees of freedom, force methods force you to track constraint forces at every joint, manage vector forces and torques in many frames, and untangle interaction forces between links. Sign errors and missing coupling terms become routine.

Energy methods work with scalars. You compute kinetic and potential energy, form the Lagrangian, and apply a fixed procedure. Constraint forces simply vanish from the final equations — they do no work on admissible motions, so the formalism eliminates them automatically.

The real advantage isn't elegance — it's that the same five steps work for a 2-DOF planar arm and a 7-DOF surgical robot. That's why every dynamics textbook and every robotics toolbox builds on Lagrange.

Newton-Euler (force-based)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector bookkeeping across frames, and large coupled systems prone to sign errors.

Lagrange (energy-based)

Scalar energies, automatic constraint elimination, generalized coordinates, and a well-defined procedure that is easy to automate.

3-DOF arm comparison

Force method: 6 equations per link plus constraint elimination. Energy method: 3 scalar $T_i$, 3 scalar $V_i$, one $L = T - V$, then Euler-Lagrange. Same answer — far less pain.

Interactive · pick a method Try this on for size: choose Newton-Euler or Lagrange for a 1-, 2-, or 3-link arm and watch the equation count, constraint forces, and frame transformations light up side by side. The two paths converge on the same equations — but one of them is dramatically shorter.
§ 2.0

Kinetic energy in multi-link systems

Energy · T

Kinetic energy in robotics is not the $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ of elementary physics. Every link has both translational kinetic energy (from its center-of-mass velocity) and rotational kinetic energy (from spinning about its center of mass), and the two are coupled through the kinematic chain.

When joint 1 moves, every subsequent link moves with it, each picking up velocity contributions from every joint between itself and the base. This is the velocity coupling that gives robot dynamics their characteristic nonlinearity and cross-terms.

Kinetic energy formula

For a robot with $n$ links: $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right]$. Here $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the CoM velocity, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ the angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ the inertia tensor about the CoM.

Where the coupling lives

Both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on the velocities of all joints from the base to link $i$. That dependency is the source of every coupling term in the inertia matrix.

Interactive · animated coupling Drive $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ on a planar arm and watch each link's translational and rotational kinetic energy stream into the total. You'll see exactly how downstream links inherit velocity from every upstream joint.
§ 3.0

Potential energy and configuration dependence

Energy · V

Potential energy in robotics is primarily gravitational and depends on position only, not velocity — which makes it considerably simpler than kinetic energy.

The key insight is that potential energy is strongly configuration-dependent. An extended horizontal arm stores far more gravitational potential energy than the same arm folded vertically, and the gradient of $V$ with respect to joint angles is exactly the gravitational torque that actuators must overcome.

Gravity compensation in any modern controller is just $\partial V / \partial q_i$ — the same quantity you'd compute by hand here. The math is the implementation.

Potential energy formula

$V = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \mathbf{g}^T \mathbf{r}_i$ where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration vector (typically $[0, 0, -9.81]^T$ m/s$^2$) and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the CoM position of link $i$.

Reference frame choice

You're free to pick any reference height; the equations of motion depend only on differences. A smart choice can collapse several terms to zero.

Interactive · build $V$ Construct $V$ for a 2-DOF planar arm by dragging each link's centre of mass to a height and watching the $m_i g h_i$ terms snap into a live sum. Then sweep $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and watch $V$ change — along with the gravity torque $\partial V/\partial q_i$ at each joint.
§ 4.0

The Lagrangian and generalized coordinates

Framework

Generalized coordinates are any independent parameters that completely specify the configuration. For robots, the natural choice is the joint variables: angles $\theta_i$ for revolute joints, displacements $d_i$ for prismatic joints. A robot with $n$ joints has $n$ degrees of freedom and $n$ generalized coordinates — a minimal, complete description.

The Lagrangian is the scalar function

$$L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q})$$

It's the difference between kinetic and potential energy. Systems evolve along the path that extremizes the time integral of $L$ (the action) — and that variational principle is exactly what produces the Euler-Lagrange equations.

Why joint variables are special

Joint coordinates are minimal (no redundant parameters), automatically satisfy kinematic constraints, and correspond directly to actuator readings — so theory and hardware speak the same language.

Interpretation

$L$ measures the excess of kinetic energy over potential energy. Nature picks trajectories that extremize the time integral of this excess.

§ 5.0

The Euler-Lagrange equations

Procedure

The Euler-Lagrange equations turn the Lagrangian into equations of motion. For each generalized coordinate $q_i$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = \tau_i$$

where $\tau_i$ is the generalized force (joint torque for revolute joints, force for prismatic). The procedure is mechanical: write $T$ and $V$, form $L = T - V$, take the required partials, and simplify.

Once you've written $L$, the rest is calculus. That's the whole appeal — derivation becomes bookkeeping, not insight.

The five-step recipe

1) Express $T$ and $V$ in generalized coordinates. 2) Form $L = T - V$. 3) Compute $\partial L / \partial \dot{q}_i$ and $\partial L / \partial q_i$. 4) Differentiate the velocity partial with respect to time. 5) Substitute into Euler-Lagrange and simplify.

Worked sketch: 2-DOF planar arm

Choose $q_1 = \theta_1$, $q_2 = \theta_2$. Link 1 rotates with $\dot{\theta}_1$; link 2 picks up coupled motion from both joints. The resulting equations are nonlinear, coupled, and capture inertial coupling, Coriolis/centrifugal effects, and gravity loading — even for this minimal system.

Interactive · derive it yourself Now you walk through the recipe. Pick a production rule at each step — write $T$, write $V$, form $L$, take partials, apply Euler-Lagrange — and the expression tree grows until you've produced the equation of motion for a 1-DOF pendulum, then a 2-DOF arm.
§ 6.0

Velocity kinematics for energy calculations

Jacobians

To compute $T$ you need link velocities, and those follow from the kinematic chain. The linear velocity of link $i$'s center of mass is

$$\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j} \dot{q}_j = \mathbf{J}_{vi}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ is the velocity Jacobian for the CoM of link $i$.

Angular velocities follow joint-type rules: a revolute joint $j$ with rate $\dot{q}_j$ contributes $\dot{q}_j$ (about its axis) to every link downstream; a prismatic joint contributes zero. So the total angular velocity of link $i$ is the vector sum of contributions from all revolute joints between it and the base.

3-DOF planar example

All revolute, planar: $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 = \dot{q}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_3 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2 + \dot{q}_3$. Each subsequent link inherits velocity from more joints — that's where coupling terms come from.

Practical takeaway

Get the Jacobians right and the kinetic energy expression writes itself. Most errors in Lagrangian derivations trace back to a sloppy velocity expression.

§ 7.0

The inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Structure

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into the kinetic energy formula yields a quadratic form in joint velocities:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is the inertia matrix (sometimes called the mass matrix), with elements

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right]$$

Reading $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Diagonal $D_{ii}$: effective inertia felt by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves. Off-diagonal $D_{ij}$: inertial coupling between joints $i$ and $j$. The whole matrix changes with configuration.

Mathematical properties

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — kinetic energy is non-negative, and zero only when $\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0}$. This guarantees physically consistent, well-posed dynamics.

Interactive · pick a configuration Slide $\theta_2$ on a 2-DOF arm and watch all four entries of the inertia matrix update in real time, with the eigenvalues plotted alongside. You'll see why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent — and where the coupling lives.
§ 8.0

Deriving the standard robot equation

Result

Plugging $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ into Euler-Lagrange and taking the required derivatives produces the standard form of the robot dynamic equation:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$$

Each term has a distinct physical origin:

  • $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ — inertial term, straight from $T$.
  • $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis and centrifugal terms, arising from the time-derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ minus the position-partial of $T$.
  • $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \partial V / \partial \mathbf{q}$ — gravitational term, from $V$.

Inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Comes directly from kinetic energy.

Coriolis/centrifugal $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$

Quadratic in velocities: $h_i = \sum_j \sum_k h_{ijk} \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k$ with Christoffel-style symbols $h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right)$.

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$

$c_i = \partial V / \partial q_i$. Conservative, velocity-independent, the literal gradient of potential energy.

Why this form matters

Every modern model-based controller — computed-torque, inverse dynamics, passivity-based — references this exact decomposition. Get $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ right and you can implement any of them.

Self-check · four short questions Before moving on, confirm you can name where each term comes from, what it depends on, and why constraint forces never appear. Get all four and you're ready for Module 3.
§ 9.0

Self-assessment: 2-DOF planar arm

Practice

System. A 2-link planar arm with both link masses concentrated at the distal end (the tip) of each link.

Parameters.

  • Link 1: length $L_1$, mass $m_1$ at its tip.
  • Link 2: length $L_2$, mass $m_2$ at its tip.
  • Joint angles $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ (with $\theta_2$ measured relative to link 1).
  • Neglect link mass distribution and link inertia — assume all mass at the tips.

Tasks.

  1. Kinematics. Write the position of each mass $(m_1, m_2)$ in terms of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$.
  2. Velocities. Compute the velocity of each mass using the chain rule and joint velocities $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.
  3. Kinetic energy. Write the total $T$ of the system (no need to expand).
  4. Potential energy. Write the total gravitational $V$, with gravity acting in the $-y$ direction.
  5. Lagrangian. Form $L = T - V$.

Draw your own schematic and label every point, velocity, and angle. The exercise looks small, but it's the same procedure you'd run on a 7-DOF industrial arm — just with more terms.

Why this exercise matters

This is the smallest non-trivial system that exhibits inertial coupling, Coriolis effects, and configuration-dependent gravity all at once. Master it and the rest scales.

§ 10.0

From theory to industrial controllers

In practice

The energy-based framework isn't an academic exercise — it's the foundation of every modern industrial robot controller. Embedded processors compute $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster as part of real-time control loops.

Downstream applications include trajectory optimization (minimum-time, minimum-energy paths), collision detection via energy monitoring, force limiting for safe human-robot interaction, and predictive maintenance from drive-torque signatures.

Performance gains in practice

Lagrangian-based control delivers position accuracy under 0.1 mm at high speed, 20–40% energy savings over basic PID, 2–3× faster cycle times, and reduced mechanical wear.

Automotive welding case study

Before (PID): ±2 mm, 45 s cycle. After (model-based): ±0.2 mm, 28 s cycle. Result: 35% faster production, 90% accuracy improvement, 25% energy savings.

Looking forward to Module 3

Next module: complete velocity formulation, systematic derivation of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, computation of $\mathbf{h}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, and full worked examples on real robot geometries.

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into the kinetic energy formula yields a quadratic form in joint velocities:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is the inertia matrix (sometimes called the mass matrix), with elements

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right]$$

Reading $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Diagonal $D_{ii}$: effective inertia felt by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves. Off-diagonal $D_{ij}$: inertial coupling between joints $i$ and $j$. The whole matrix changes with configuration.

Mathematical properties

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — kinetic energy is non-negative, and zero only when $\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0}$. This guarantees physically consistent, well-posed dynamics.

Interactive · pick a configuration Slide $\theta_2$ on a 2-DOF arm and watch all four entries of the inertia matrix update in real time, with the eigenvalues plotted alongside. You'll see why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent — and where the coupling lives.
§ 8.0

Deriving the standard robot equation

Result

Plugging $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ into Euler-Lagrange and taking the required derivatives produces the standard form of the robot dynamic equation:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$$

Each term has a distinct physical origin:

  • $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ — inertial term, straight from $T$.
  • $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis and centrifugal terms, arising from the time-derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ minus the position-partial of $T$.
  • $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \partial V / \partial \mathbf{q}$ — gravitational term, from $V$.

Inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Comes directly from kinetic energy.

Coriolis/centrifugal $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$

Quadratic in velocities: $h_i = \sum_j \sum_k h_{ijk} \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k$ with Christoffel-style symbols $h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right)$.

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$

$c_i = \partial V / \partial q_i$. Conservative, velocity-independent, the literal gradient of potential energy.

Why this form matters

Every modern model-based controller — computed-torque, inverse dynamics, passivity-based — references this exact decomposition. Get $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ right and you can implement any of them.

Self-check · four short questions Before moving on, confirm you can name where each term comes from, what it depends on, and why constraint forces never appear. Get all four and you're ready for Module 3.
§ 9.0

Self-assessment: 2-DOF planar arm

Practice

System. A 2-link planar arm with both link masses concentrated at the distal end (the tip) of each link.

Parameters.

  • Link 1: length $L_1$, mass $m_1$ at its tip.
  • Link 2: length $L_2$, mass $m_2$ at its tip.
  • Joint angles $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ (with $\theta_2$ measured relative to link 1).
  • Neglect link mass distribution and link inertia — assume all mass at the tips.

Tasks.

  1. Kinematics. Write the position of each mass $(m_1, m_2)$ in terms of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$.
  2. Velocities. Compute the velocity of each mass using the chain rule and joint velocities $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.
  3. Kinetic energy. Write the total $T$ of the system (no need to expand).
  4. Potential energy. Write the total gravitational $V$, with gravity acting in the $-y$ direction.
  5. Lagrangian. Form $L = T - V$.

Draw your own schematic and label every point, velocity, and angle. The exercise looks small, but it's the same procedure you'd run on a 7-DOF industrial arm — just with more terms.

Why this exercise matters

This is the smallest non-trivial system that exhibits inertial coupling, Coriolis effects, and configuration-dependent gravity all at once. Master it and the rest scales.

§ 10.0

From theory to industrial controllers

In practice

The energy-based framework isn't an academic exercise — it's the foundation of every modern industrial robot controller. Embedded processors compute $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster as part of real-time control loops.

Downstream applications include trajectory optimization (minimum-time, minimum-energy paths), collision detection via energy monitoring, force limiting for safe human-robot interaction, and predictive maintenance from drive-torque signatures.

Performance gains in practice

Lagrangian-based control delivers position accuracy under 0.1 mm at high speed, 20–40% energy savings over basic PID, 2–3× faster cycle times, and reduced mechanical wear.

Automotive welding case study

Before (PID): ±2 mm, 45 s cycle. After (model-based): ±0.2 mm, 28 s cycle. Result: 35% faster production, 90% accuracy improvement, 25% energy savings.

Looking forward to Module 3

Next module: complete velocity formulation, systematic derivation of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, computation of $\mathbf{h}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, and full worked examples on real robot geometries.

Lagrangian mechanics and systematic dynamic modeling for multi-link manipulators.

By the end you'll see why $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ falls out almost automatically — and why every modern industrial controller is built on top of this idea.

§ 0.0

What this lecture covers

Orientation

This module builds the energy-based framework for robot dynamics. We start by asking why energy methods beat force methods for multi-link systems, then assemble the pieces: kinetic and potential energy for a kinematic chain, generalized coordinates, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, and the Euler-Lagrange equations.

From there we'll see how velocity kinematics feed the kinetic energy expression, how the inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ emerges as a quadratic form, and how the standard robot equation $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ falls out of the derivation — with each term having a clear physical meaning.

We close with a self-assessment on a 2-DOF planar arm and a look at how this theory powers real industrial controllers.

Think of this as the moment robot dynamics stops being a wall of free-body diagrams and starts being something you can derive systematically — even for arms you've never seen before.

Learning objectives

Master energy fundamentals, the Lagrangian framework, generalized coordinates, Euler-Lagrange equations, and the systematic derivation of robot dynamic equations.

§ 1.0

Why energy methods beat force methods

Motivation

Force-based and energy-based dynamics are mathematically equivalent — they produce the same final equations. The difference is the path to those equations.

For a single pendulum or a particle, Newton-Euler is intuitive: draw the free-body diagram, sum forces, done. But once you have a multi-link robot with several degrees of freedom, force methods force you to track constraint forces at every joint, manage vector forces and torques in many frames, and untangle interaction forces between links. Sign errors and missing coupling terms become routine.

Energy methods work with scalars. You compute kinetic and potential energy, form the Lagrangian, and apply a fixed procedure. Constraint forces simply vanish from the final equations — they do no work on admissible motions, so the formalism eliminates them automatically.

The real advantage isn't elegance — it's that the same five steps work for a 2-DOF planar arm and a 7-DOF surgical robot. That's why every dynamics textbook and every robotics toolbox builds on Lagrange.

Newton-Euler (force-based)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector bookkeeping across frames, and large coupled systems prone to sign errors.

Lagrange (energy-based)

Scalar energies, automatic constraint elimination, generalized coordinates, and a well-defined procedure that is easy to automate.

3-DOF arm comparison

Force method: 6 equations per link plus constraint elimination. Energy method: 3 scalar $T_i$, 3 scalar $V_i$, one $L = T - V$, then Euler-Lagrange. Same answer — far less pain.

Interactive · pick a method Try this on for size: choose Newton-Euler or Lagrange for a 1-, 2-, or 3-link arm and watch the equation count, constraint forces, and frame transformations light up side by side. The two paths converge on the same equations — but one of them is dramatically shorter.
§ 2.0

Kinetic energy in multi-link systems

Energy · T

Kinetic energy in robotics is not the $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ of elementary physics. Every link has both translational kinetic energy (from its center-of-mass velocity) and rotational kinetic energy (from spinning about its center of mass), and the two are coupled through the kinematic chain.

When joint 1 moves, every subsequent link moves with it, each picking up velocity contributions from every joint between itself and the base. This is the velocity coupling that gives robot dynamics their characteristic nonlinearity and cross-terms.

Kinetic energy formula

For a robot with $n$ links: $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right]$. Here $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the CoM velocity, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ the angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ the inertia tensor about the CoM.

Where the coupling lives

Both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on the velocities of all joints from the base to link $i$. That dependency is the source of every coupling term in the inertia matrix.

Interactive · animated coupling Drive $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ on a planar arm and watch each link's translational and rotational kinetic energy stream into the total. You'll see exactly how downstream links inherit velocity from every upstream joint.
§ 3.0

Potential energy and configuration dependence

Energy · V

Potential energy in robotics is primarily gravitational and depends on position only, not velocity — which makes it considerably simpler than kinetic energy.

The key insight is that potential energy is strongly configuration-dependent. An extended horizontal arm stores far more gravitational potential energy than the same arm folded vertically, and the gradient of $V$ with respect to joint angles is exactly the gravitational torque that actuators must overcome.

Gravity compensation in any modern controller is just $\partial V / \partial q_i$ — the same quantity you'd compute by hand here. The math is the implementation.

Potential energy formula

$V = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \mathbf{g}^T \mathbf{r}_i$ where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration vector (typically $[0, 0, -9.81]^T$ m/s$^2$) and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the CoM position of link $i$.

Reference frame choice

You're free to pick any reference height; the equations of motion depend only on differences. A smart choice can collapse several terms to zero.

Interactive · build $V$ Construct $V$ for a 2-DOF planar arm by dragging each link's centre of mass to a height and watching the $m_i g h_i$ terms snap into a live sum. Then sweep $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and watch $V$ change — along with the gravity torque $\partial V/\partial q_i$ at each joint.
§ 4.0

The Lagrangian and generalized coordinates

Framework

Generalized coordinates are any independent parameters that completely specify the configuration. For robots, the natural choice is the joint variables: angles $\theta_i$ for revolute joints, displacements $d_i$ for prismatic joints. A robot with $n$ joints has $n$ degrees of freedom and $n$ generalized coordinates — a minimal, complete description.

The Lagrangian is the scalar function

$$L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q})$$

It's the difference between kinetic and potential energy. Systems evolve along the path that extremizes the time integral of $L$ (the action) — and that variational principle is exactly what produces the Euler-Lagrange equations.

Why joint variables are special

Joint coordinates are minimal (no redundant parameters), automatically satisfy kinematic constraints, and correspond directly to actuator readings — so theory and hardware speak the same language.

Interpretation

$L$ measures the excess of kinetic energy over potential energy. Nature picks trajectories that extremize the time integral of this excess.

§ 5.0

The Euler-Lagrange equations

Procedure

The Euler-Lagrange equations turn the Lagrangian into equations of motion. For each generalized coordinate $q_i$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = \tau_i$$

where $\tau_i$ is the generalized force (joint torque for revolute joints, force for prismatic). The procedure is mechanical: write $T$ and $V$, form $L = T - V$, take the required partials, and simplify.

Once you've written $L$, the rest is calculus. That's the whole appeal — derivation becomes bookkeeping, not insight.

The five-step recipe

1) Express $T$ and $V$ in generalized coordinates. 2) Form $L = T - V$. 3) Compute $\partial L / \partial \dot{q}_i$ and $\partial L / \partial q_i$. 4) Differentiate the velocity partial with respect to time. 5) Substitute into Euler-Lagrange and simplify.

Worked sketch: 2-DOF planar arm

Choose $q_1 = \theta_1$, $q_2 = \theta_2$. Link 1 rotates with $\dot{\theta}_1$; link 2 picks up coupled motion from both joints. The resulting equations are nonlinear, coupled, and capture inertial coupling, Coriolis/centrifugal effects, and gravity loading — even for this minimal system.

Interactive · derive it yourself Now you walk through the recipe. Pick a production rule at each step — write $T$, write $V$, form $L$, take partials, apply Euler-Lagrange — and the expression tree grows until you've produced the equation of motion for a 1-DOF pendulum, then a 2-DOF arm.
§ 6.0

Velocity kinematics for energy calculations

Jacobians

To compute $T$ you need link velocities, and those follow from the kinematic chain. The linear velocity of link $i$'s center of mass is

$$\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j} \dot{q}_j = \mathbf{J}_{vi}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ is the velocity Jacobian for the CoM of link $i$.

Angular velocities follow joint-type rules: a revolute joint $j$ with rate $\dot{q}_j$ contributes $\dot{q}_j$ (about its axis) to every link downstream; a prismatic joint contributes zero. So the total angular velocity of link $i$ is the vector sum of contributions from all revolute joints between it and the base.

3-DOF planar example

All revolute, planar: $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 = \dot{q}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_3 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2 + \dot{q}_3$. Each subsequent link inherits velocity from more joints — that's where coupling terms come from.

Practical takeaway

Get the Jacobians right and the kinetic energy expression writes itself. Most errors in Lagrangian derivations trace back to a sloppy velocity expression.

§ 7.0

The inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Structure

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into the kinetic energy formula yields a quadratic form in joint velocities:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is the inertia matrix (sometimes called the mass matrix), with elements

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right]$$

Reading $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Diagonal $D_{ii}$: effective inertia felt by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves. Off-diagonal $D_{ij}$: inertial coupling between joints $i$ and $j$. The whole matrix changes with configuration.

Mathematical properties

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — kinetic energy is non-negative, and zero only when $\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0}$. This guarantees physically consistent, well-posed dynamics.

Interactive · pick a configuration Slide $\theta_2$ on a 2-DOF arm and watch all four entries of the inertia matrix update in real time, with the eigenvalues plotted alongside. You'll see why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent — and where the coupling lives.
§ 8.0

Deriving the standard robot equation

Result

Plugging $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ into Euler-Lagrange and taking the required derivatives produces the standard form of the robot dynamic equation:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$$

Each term has a distinct physical origin:

  • $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ — inertial term, straight from $T$.
  • $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis and centrifugal terms, arising from the time-derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ minus the position-partial of $T$.
  • $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \partial V / \partial \mathbf{q}$ — gravitational term, from $V$.

Inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Comes directly from kinetic energy.

Coriolis/centrifugal $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$

Quadratic in velocities: $h_i = \sum_j \sum_k h_{ijk} \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k$ with Christoffel-style symbols $h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right)$.

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$

$c_i = \partial V / \partial q_i$. Conservative, velocity-independent, the literal gradient of potential energy.

Why this form matters

Every modern model-based controller — computed-torque, inverse dynamics, passivity-based — references this exact decomposition. Get $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ right and you can implement any of them.

Self-check · four short questions Before moving on, confirm you can name where each term comes from, what it depends on, and why constraint forces never appear. Get all four and you're ready for Module 3.

Parameters.

  • Link 1: length $L_1$, mass $m_1$ at its tip.
  • Link 2: length $L_2$, mass $m_2$ at its tip.
  • Joint angles $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ (with $\theta_2$ measured relative to link 1).
  • Neglect link mass distribution and link inertia — assume all mass at the tips.

Tasks.

  1. Kinematics. Write the position of each mass $(m_1, m_2)$ in terms of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$.
  2. Velocities. Compute the velocity of each mass using the chain rule and joint velocities $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.
  3. Kinetic energy. Write the total $T$ of the system (no need to expand).
  4. Potential energy. Write the total gravitational $V$, with gravity acting in the $-y$ direction.

Draw your own schematic and label every point, velocity, and angle. The exercise looks small, but it's the same procedure you'd run on a 7-DOF industrial arm — just with more terms.

Why this exercise matters

This is the smallest non-trivial system that exhibits inertial coupling, Coriolis effects, and configuration-dependent gravity all at once. Master it and the rest scales.

The energy-based framework isn't an academic exercise — it's the foundation of every modern industrial robot controller. Embedded processors compute $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster as part of real-time control loops.

Motivation

The real advantage isn't elegance — it's that the same five steps work for a 2-DOF planar arm and a 7-DOF surgical robot. That's why every dynamics textbook and every robotics toolbox builds on Lagrange.

Newton-Euler (force-based)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector bookkeeping across frames, and large coupled systems prone to sign errors.

Lagrange (energy-based)

Scalar energies, automatic constraint elimination, generalized coordinates, and a well-defined procedure that is easy to automate.

§ 2.0

Kinetic energy in multi-link systems

Energy · T

Kinetic energy in robotics is not the $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ of elementary physics. Every link has both translational kinetic energy (from its center-of-mass velocity) and rotational kinetic energy (from spinning about its center of mass), and the two are coupled through the kinematic chain.

When joint 1 moves, every subsequent link moves with it, each picking up velocity contributions from every joint between itself and the base. This is the velocity coupling that gives robot dynamics their characteristic nonlinearity and cross-terms.

Kinetic energy formula

For a robot with $n$ links: $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right]$. Here $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the CoM velocity, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ the angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ the inertia tensor about the CoM.

Where the coupling lives

Both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on the velocities of all joints from the base to link $i$. That dependency is the source of every coupling term in the inertia matrix.

Interactive · animated coupling Drive $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ on a planar arm and watch each link's translational and rotational kinetic energy stream into the total. You'll see exactly how downstream links inherit velocity from every upstream joint.
§ 3.0

Potential energy and configuration dependence

Energy · V

Potential energy in robotics is primarily gravitational and depends on position only, not velocity — which makes it considerably simpler than kinetic energy.

The key insight is that potential energy is strongly configuration-dependent. An extended horizontal arm stores far more gravitational potential energy than the same arm folded vertically, and the gradient of $V$ with respect to joint angles is exactly the gravitational torque that actuators must overcome.

Gravity compensation in any modern controller is just $\partial V / \partial q_i$ — the same quantity you'd compute by hand here. The math is the implementation.

Potential energy formula

$V = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \mathbf{g}^T \mathbf{r}_i$ where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration vector (typically $[0, 0, -9.81]^T$ m/s$^2$) and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the CoM position of link $i$.

Reference frame choice

You're free to pick any reference height; the equations of motion depend only on differences. A smart choice can collapse several terms to zero.

Interactive · build $V$ Construct $V$ for a 2-DOF planar arm by dragging each link's centre of mass to a height and watching the $m_i g h_i$ terms snap into a live sum. Then sweep $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and watch $V$ change — along with the gravity torque $\partial V/\partial q_i$ at each joint.
§ 4.0

The Lagrangian and generalized coordinates

Framework

Generalized coordinates are any independent parameters that completely specify the configuration. For robots, the natural choice is the joint variables: angles $\theta_i$ for revolute joints, displacements $d_i$ for prismatic joints. A robot with $n$ joints has $n$ degrees of freedom and $n$ generalized coordinates — a minimal, complete description.

The Lagrangian is the scalar function

$$L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q})$$

It's the difference between kinetic and potential energy. Systems evolve along the path that extremizes the time integral of $L$ (the action) — and that variational principle is exactly what produces the Euler-Lagrange equations.

Why joint variables are special

Joint coordinates are minimal (no redundant parameters), automatically satisfy kinematic constraints, and correspond directly to actuator readings — so theory and hardware speak the same language.

Interpretation

$L$ measures the excess of kinetic energy over potential energy. Nature picks trajectories that extremize the time integral of this excess.

§ 5.0

The Euler-Lagrange equations

Procedure

The Euler-Lagrange equations turn the Lagrangian into equations of motion. For each generalized coordinate $q_i$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = \tau_i$$

where $\tau_i$ is the generalized force (joint torque for revolute joints, force for prismatic). The procedure is mechanical: write $T$ and $V$, form $L = T - V$, take the required partials, and simplify.

Once you've written $L$, the rest is calculus. That's the whole appeal — derivation becomes bookkeeping, not insight.

The five-step recipe

1) Express $T$ and $V$ in generalized coordinates. 2) Form $L = T - V$. 3) Compute $\partial L / \partial \dot{q}_i$ and $\partial L / \partial q_i$. 4) Differentiate the velocity partial with respect to time. 5) Substitute into Euler-Lagrange and simplify.

Worked sketch: 2-DOF planar arm

Choose $q_1 = \theta_1$, $q_2 = \theta_2$. Link 1 rotates with $\dot{\theta}_1$; link 2 picks up coupled motion from both joints. The resulting equations are nonlinear, coupled, and capture inertial coupling, Coriolis/centrifugal effects, and gravity loading — even for this minimal system.

Interactive · derive it yourself Now you walk through the recipe. Pick a production rule at each step — write $T$, write $V$, form $L$, take partials, apply Euler-Lagrange — and the expression tree grows until you've produced the equation of motion for a 1-DOF pendulum, then a 2-DOF arm.
§ 6.0

Velocity kinematics for energy calculations

Jacobians

To compute $T$ you need link velocities, and those follow from the kinematic chain. The linear velocity of link $i$'s center of mass is

$$\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j} \dot{q}_j = \mathbf{J}_{vi}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ is the velocity Jacobian for the CoM of link $i$.

Angular velocities follow joint-type rules: a revolute joint $j$ with rate $\dot{q}_j$ contributes $\dot{q}_j$ (about its axis) to every link downstream; a prismatic joint contributes zero. So the total angular velocity of link $i$ is the vector sum of contributions from all revolute joints between it and the base.

3-DOF planar example

All revolute, planar: $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 = \dot{q}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_3 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2 + \dot{q}_3$. Each subsequent link inherits velocity from more joints — that's where coupling terms come from.

Practical takeaway

Get the Jacobians right and the kinetic energy expression writes itself. Most errors in Lagrangian derivations trace back to a sloppy velocity expression.

§ 7.0

The inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Structure

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into the kinetic energy formula yields a quadratic form in joint velocities:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is the inertia matrix (sometimes called the mass matrix), with elements

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^T \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right]$$

Reading $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Diagonal $D_{ii}$: effective inertia felt by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves. Off-diagonal $D_{ij}$: inertial coupling between joints $i$ and $j$. The whole matrix changes with configuration.

Mathematical properties

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — kinetic energy is non-negative, and zero only when $\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0}$. This guarantees physically consistent, well-posed dynamics.

Interactive · pick a configuration Slide $\theta_2$ on a 2-DOF arm and watch all four entries of the inertia matrix update in real time, with the eigenvalues plotted alongside. You'll see why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent — and where the coupling lives.
§ 8.0

Deriving the standard robot equation

Result

Plugging $T = \tfrac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ into Euler-Lagrange and taking the required derivatives produces the standard form of the robot dynamic equation:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$$

Each term has a distinct physical origin:

  • $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ — inertial term, straight from $T$.
  • $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis and centrifugal terms, arising from the time-derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ minus the position-partial of $T$.
  • $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \partial V / \partial \mathbf{q}$ — gravitational term, from $V$.

Inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Comes directly from kinetic energy.

Coriolis/centrifugal $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$

Quadratic in velocities: $h_i = \sum_j \sum_k h_{ijk} \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k$ with Christoffel-style symbols $h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right)$.

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$

$c_i = \partial V / \partial q_i$. Conservative, velocity-independent, the literal gradient of potential energy.

Why this form matters

Every modern model-based controller — computed-torque, inverse dynamics, passivity-based — references this exact decomposition. Get $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ right and you can implement any of them.

Self-check · four short questions Before moving on, confirm you can name where each term comes from, what it depends on, and why constraint forces never appear. Get all four and you're ready for Module 3.
§ 9.0

Self-assessment: 2-DOF planar arm

Practice

System. A 2-link planar arm with both link masses concentrated at the distal end (the tip) of each link.

Parameters.

  • Link 1: length $L_1$, mass $m_1$ at its tip.
  • Link 2: length $L_2$, mass $m_2$ at its tip.
  • Joint angles $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ (with $\theta_2$ measured relative to link 1).
  • Neglect link mass distribution and link inertia — assume all mass at the tips.

Tasks.

  1. Kinematics. Write the position of each mass $(m_1, m_2)$ in terms of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$.
  2. Velocities. Compute the velocity of each mass using the chain rule and joint velocities $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.
  3. Kinetic energy. Write the total $T$ of the system (no need to expand).
  4. Potential energy. Write the total gravitational $V$, with gravity acting in the $-y$ direction.
  5. Lagrangian. Form $L = T - V$.

Draw your own schematic and label every point, velocity, and angle. The exercise looks small, but it's the same procedure you'd run on a 7-DOF industrial arm — just with more terms.

Why this exercise matters

This is the smallest non-trivial system that exhibits inertial coupling, Coriolis effects, and configuration-dependent gravity all at once. Master it and the rest scales.

§ 10.0

From theory to industrial controllers

In practice

The energy-based framework isn't an academic exercise — it's the foundation of every modern industrial robot controller. Embedded processors compute $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster as part of real-time control loops.

Downstream applications include trajectory optimization (minimum-time, minimum-energy paths), collision detection via energy monitoring, force limiting for safe human-robot interaction, and predictive maintenance from drive-torque signatures.

Performance gains in practice

Lagrangian-based control delivers position accuracy under 0.1 mm at high speed, 20–40% energy savings over basic PID, 2–3× faster cycle times, and reduced mechanical wear.

Automotive welding case study

Before (PID): ±2 mm, 45 s cycle. After (model-based): ±0.2 mm, 28 s cycle. Result: 35% faster production, 90% accuracy improvement, 25% energy savings.

Looking forward to Module 3

Next module: complete velocity formulation, systematic derivation of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, computation of $\mathbf{h}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, and full worked examples on real robot geometries.

Assemble $L = T - V$ for the 2-DOF arm. Identify which terms will produce inertial coupling, which will produce Coriolis/centrifugal effects, and which will produce gravity terms once Euler-Lagrange is applied.
